events.title: Fulton's Steamboat Begins Its Hudson River Voyage
events.description: Robert Fulton's North River Steamboat, later known as the Clermont, left New York City for Albany. The trip launched the first commercial steamboat service in the world.
events.significance: Steam-powered river travel made transport faster and more reliable. It helped speed up trade and westward expansion in the United States.

events.title: Birth of Marcus Garvey
events.description: Marcus Garvey was born in St. Ann's Bay, Jamaica. He grew up to become a publisher, orator and organizer who promoted Black pride and economic self-reliance.
events.significance: His Universal Negro Improvement Association became one of the largest Black mass movements in history. It influenced later civil rights and independence leaders around the world.

events.title: Indonesia Proclaims Independence
events.description: Two days after Japan's surrender in World War II, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta declared Indonesia's independence in Jakarta. The declaration set off a four-year struggle against Dutch efforts to reclaim the colony.
events.significance: Indonesia is now the world's fourth most populous nation. Its independence is a landmark in the wave of decolonization after the war.

events.title: Hurricane Camille Strikes the U.S. Gulf Coast
events.description: Hurricane Camille made landfall along the Mississippi coast as one of the most powerful storms ever to hit the United States. It killed 243 people, mostly through storm surge and flooding.
events.significance: Camille drove major advances in hurricane forecasting, evacuation planning and building practices along the Gulf Coast.

events.title: Clinton Addresses the Nation on the Lewinsky Affair
events.description: President Bill Clinton testified to a grand jury and then spoke to the nation in a televised address. He admitted an inappropriate relationship with Monica Lewinsky.
events.significance: The admission deepened the scandal that led to Clinton's impeachment by the House of Representatives in December 1998.
